div.p: In this paper, we are interested in the energyefficient scheduling of real-time tasks which may access lockfree objects in a non-ideal DVS processor. We propose an algorithm, called interference-aware speed assignment (IASA), to assign proper execution speeds to tasks which are scheduled by the earliest deadline first (EDF) scheduling policy. The execution speeds are calculated based on the schedulability analysis of the EDF policy with the cost of lock-free objects' retry loops. As a result, the energy consumption can be reduced while satisfying the timing constraints of real-time tasks. Our experimental results show that the IASA algorithm is very effective in energy saving.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Many embedded real-time applications involve concurrent accesses to shared data objects, resulting in contention for those objects. Researchers have proposed excellent real-time synchronization protocols to resolve such a contention problem. Those protocols can be classified into two categories: lock-based and lock-free. In the literatures, most protocols are lock-based which permits concurrent accesses to data objects by resorting to critical sections protected by locks. Lock-based protocols have several disadvantages such as the concurrency is reduced due to serialized access to data objects, and priority inversion occurs when a higher-priority task must wait on another lower-priority task to release the lock on a data object. Such disadvantages have motivated the research on lock-free protocols.

When lock-free protocols are employed, shared data objects are implemented as lock-free objects which can be concurrently accessed without locks. Typically, an operation on a lock-free object continuously accesses the object, checks, and retries until it becomes successful. Such an operation is usually implemented by using the retry loop. The retry loop of a lock-free object usually implemented by using a compare-andswap (CAS) instruction to atomically update of the object. An important property of lock-free objects is that the operations may interfere with each other. An interference occurs when a successful retry loop by a task results in a failed retry loop by another task. Although the disadvantages of lock-based protocols can be overcome by using lock-free objects. The access of a lock-free object may take arbitrarily long time to complete due to the repeated interferences.

The research on lock-free synchronization for real-time systems have started by Sorensen and Hemachar [1] and Kopetz and Reisinger [2]. Based on their results, researchers have subsequently presented excellent lock-free synchronization approaches and schedulability analyses for real-time systems (such as [3], [4], [5], [6], [7]). In particular, Anderson et al. [6], [7] showed how to bound the retry loops of lock-free protocols through judicious scheduling.

Nowadays, many processors are deployed with dynamic voltage scaling (DVS) supports. One of the most critical design issues of battery-driven real-time embedded systems is how to reduce energy consumption so that the battery life can be prolonged. A simple way to reduce energy consumption is to slowdown the DVS processor (i.e., tasks are executed at lower processor speeds) when it is not fully utilized. However, this simple approach will cause an impact on performance due to the late completion of tasks. However, the late completion is allowed as long as the real-time tasks meet their timing requirements (e.g., their deadlines). It provides a strong driving force in energy-efficient scheduling of real-time tasks. Comprehensive surveys of energy-efficient DVS scheduling of real-time tasks can be found in [8], [9].

In this paper, we are interested in energy-efficient scheduling of real-time tasks which may access shared lock-free objects in a non-ideal DVS processor. Only a very few studies (such as [10], [11]) have been carried out in this research direction. Hunt et al. [10] examined the relationship between the performance and energy consumption of various data structures which are implemented as lock-free and lock-based objects. Their results showed that the lock-free implementations perform better and use less energy than the lockbased implementations. Lai et al. [11] proposed a lock-free utility accrual algorithm to minimize the energy consumption of tasks with the (m, k, p)-constraint and lock-free objects, where (m, k, p) specifies the requirement which at least m task deadlines out of k consecutive tasks must be met with p probability. Different from those work, we consider the wellknown periodic task model of Liu and Layland [12] with a set of shared lock-free objects. We assume that tasks are dynamic priority and scheduled by the earliest deadline first (EDF) [12] scheduling policy. An algorithm, called interference-aware speed assignment (IASA) algorithm, is proposed to calculate proper execution speeds for task execution. Note that the execution speeds calculated by the IASA are based on the schedulability analysis of tasks with the cost of objects' retry loops so that the energy consumption can be reduced while satisfying the timing constraints of tasks. The capabilities of the IASA algorithm were also evaluated by a series of experiments. The results show that the IASA algorithm is very effective in energy-efficiency.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows: Section II presents the system and task models. Section III presents the IASA algorithm. Section IV reports the experimental results. Finally, Section V is the conclusion.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL AND PROBLEM DEFINITIONS A. DVS Processor Models

The power consumption of a DVS processor can be defined as a function P C(s) of the adopted processor speed s. In the literatures, various power consumption functions of practical DVS processor have been modeled, such as [13], [14], [15], [16], [17]. div.head: B. Task Models and Lock-Free Objects
div.p: We consider a real-time system which consists of a set of n periodic tasks T = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n }. A periodic task τ i is defined by a four tuples (A i , C i , T i , D i ), where A i is the arrival time, C i is the worst-case computation amount, T i is the period, and D i is the relative deadline of task τ i . Each task τ i is a template of its instances and each instance will arrive regularly for every period T i . Let τ i,j denote the jth instance of task τ i . The arrival time of τ i,j is denoted by A i,j = A i + (j -1)T i . When a task τ i is executed at a processor speed s j , the worst-case execution time of τ i is Cj sj . Note that the worst-case execution time of the task could be C i if the task is executed at the maximum processor speed s max . A task instance τ i,j must be completed no later than its absolute deadline D i,j which is defined as its arrival time plus the relative deadline, i.e., D i,j = A i,j + D i . We consider well formed tasks which satisfy 0 ≤ C i ≤ D i ≤ T i , ∀τ i ∈ T . Note that we also assume that the relative deadline is equal to the period, i.e., D i = T i for every task τ i ∈ T .

We assume that tasks share a set of m lock-free objects O = {o 1 , o 2 , . . . , o m } which are implemented by using lockfree algorithms. Let ρ j be the execution time for one loop iteration in the implementation of a lock-free object o j , and ρ * = max 1≤j≤m {ρ j } be the worst-case (maximum) execution time of a retry loop for any object. We also define
div.formula: O A (τ i ) =< o a i,1 , o a i,2 , • • • , o a i,ni
div.p: > as the list of lock-free objects which are accessed by τ i , where o a i,j is the jth lock-free object that is accessed by τ i . Note that we use |o a i,j | denotes the accessing time (i.e., length) of the jth lock-free object of τ i .
We assume that tasks can be preempted at arbitrary points during their executions, and we ignore system overheads (such as context switch times, interrupt handler overheads, etc.)

div.head: C. Problem Definitions
div.p: Definition 1: A task instance is interfered with (or experiences an interference) if it executes a lock-free retry loop that does not successfully complete.
Definition 2: A given task set is schedulable if and only if all task instances of all tasks meet their deadlines.

Let lcm denotes the least common multiple of all tasks' periods (also called hyperperiod). Since the task set T repeats an identical execution trace every hyperperiod, we only need to examine the time interval (0, lcm] for analyzing the performance and schedulability of the entire schedule ( [12]). The research problem is as follows:

Problem 1: Energy-Efficient Scheduling of Real-Time Tasks with Lock-Free Shared Objects Given a set of n hard real-time tasks T and a set of m lockfree shared objects O. The problem is to schedule T on a nonideal DVS processor which supports a set of k discrete speeds S. During a given time interval (0, lcm], the objective of this problem is to generate a schedule such that all instances of all tasks can meet their timing requirements (i.e., their deadlines) and the energy consumption lcm 0 P C(s(t)) dt is minimized. The primary goal of this research is to guarantee that all tasks meet their deadlines, and then try to derive proper processor speeds for tasks' executions so that the energy consumption can be reduced.

div.head: A. Schedulability and the Base Processor Speed
div.p: In this paper, the given set of real-time tasks will be scheduled by the EDF scheduling policy. Hence, we shall analyze the schedulability of the EDF policy for tasks with lock-free objects, and then derive the lowest processor speed, called base processor speed, for executing tasks while guaranteeing the schedulability.

Lemma 1: A task instance can be interfered with at most once during any interval when it is preempted. Proof. According to Definition 1, a task instance will experience an interference only if it fails the execution of a retry loop for a lock-free object. Consider a task instance τ i,j which will access a lock-free object o k during its execution. Suppose that τ i,j is preempted at time t 1 by another task instance τ x,y which has a deadline earlier than τ i,j 's deadline (i.e., the priority of τ x,y is higher than that of τ i,j ), and then later τ i,j resumes its execution at time t 2 . Consider the following two cases:

Case 1: If the lock-free object o k has been accessed by τ x,y or other higher-priority tasks which preempt τ x,y during the interval [t 1 , t 2 ), τ i,j 's execution of the retry loop will be failed. As the result, τ i,j experiences an interference when it is preempted.

Case 2: If o k does not be accessed by other tasks during the interval [t 1 , t 2 ), τ i,j 's execution of the retry loop can be completed successfully. Hence, τ i,j will not be interfered with during the preempted interval.
According to the above two cases, τ i,j can be interfered with at most once during its preempted interval.

Thus, o k is one of the lock-free objects in ObjA(τ x,y ). Under the IASA algorithm, the execution speed s * i,j is assigned to the task instance τ i,j when it becomes the highest-priority task (i.e., the time it has the earliest absolute deadline among all ready tasks), and then τ i,j starts its execution at the speed s * i,j till it completes.

div.head: IV. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
div.p: The performance of our proposed IASA algorithm is compared with three approaches: maximum processor speed (MPS), base processor speed (BPS), and improved multi-speed (IMS) [18]. The MPS is the baseline approach, it always use the maximum processor speed for task execution. Under the BPS, tasks are always executed at the base processor speed s b which can be calculated by Equation (2). Note that both the MPS and the BPS algorithms use EDF as their scheduling policy. Also note that the IASA, MPS, and BPS are designed for tasks with lock-free objects. The IMS algorithm is originally designed for tasks with lock-based objects implemented using the SRP [19]. Under the IMS, all tasks are executed at a processor speed s L initially. Whenever a task τ i is blocked by another lower-priority task τ m , the processor will operate at a higher processor speed s m from the beginning of the blocking to the deadline of the blocked task or the time that the processor becomes idle. The speeds s L and s m are calculated as follows:
div.formula: s L = min sj ∈S {s j | n i=1 C i T i ≤ s j }(5)
div.p: and
div.formula: s m = max 1≤k≤m {min sj ∈S {s j | k i=1 C i T i + B m T k ≤ s j }}(6)
div.p: Where the B m is the worst-case blocking time of a task τ m . Note that the IMS also use the EDF as its scheduling policy. For ease of comparison, the energy consumption of evaluated approaches were normalized with respect to the baseline approach, i.e., the MPS algorithm (tasks are always executed at the maximum processor speed.).

div.head: A. Performance Metrics and Data Set
div.p: We have implemented a simulation of a non-ideal DVS environment to schedule different task sets. In our simulation, the speeds of the DVS processor are from 0.05 to 1 increased by 0.05, i.e., s min =s 1 =0.05, s 2 =0.1, s 3 =0.15, . . . , s 20 =s max =1.

The primary performance metric of interest is the energy consumption of tasks, referred to as EnergyConsum. The EnergyConsum is the sum of the energy consumption of every task instance executed during the simulation time. We assume that the power consumption function of processor speed be P C(s i ) = (0.08 + 1.52s 3 i ) Watts ( [16]). The energy consumption EnergyConsum can be calculated by SimT ime 0 P C(s(t)) dt, where s(t) and SimT ime are the processor speed at time t and the simulation time. Table II shows the parameters of the task sets which were evaluated in our experiments.

Recall that we use the EDF as the scheduling policy for the evaluated approaches. In order to guarantee the feasibility of generated task sets, we set the utilization factors from 0.1 to 1 (with an increment of 0.1). This is because the utilization bound for the EDF is 1 [12]. To generate a feasible task set T for a given utilization factor f , we start the empty task set and add a randomly generated task to T one by one until τi∈T Ci+ρ * Ti > f, where the value of ρ * is set as 4ms.

The execution time of a retry loop in the implementation of all lock-free objects are assumed to be the same for simplicity. Note that the last-added task was removed so that the utilization of the generated task set never exceeds f . Each generated task has a period and a computation amount selected randomly from 100ms to 2000ms and 10ms to 300ms, respectively. In our simulation, there are 5 to 10 lock-free objects. This setting provides a sufficient number of resource conflicts during the executions of tasks such that the capability of scheduling approaches can be better understand. Note that for the IMS algorithm, each lock-free object is transformed to a corresponding lock-based object which is guarded by a semaphore. For each generated task τ i , the positions and the lengths of the access of lock-free objects (or the corresponding lockbased objects for the IMS algorithm) were selected randomly under the constraint of our(τ i ) ≤ maxOU R. Where our(τ i ) is the object usage ratio of a task τ i , and maxOU R is the maximum object usage ratio of tasks. Note that the object usage ratio our(τ i ) of a task τ i is defined by (

The simulation time is 1, 000, 000ms and over 10 feasible task sets for each utilization factor with different values of the maximum object usage ratio were evaluated in the experiments and their results were averaged.

div.head: B. Experimental Results
div.p: Figures 3 shows the experimental results for the randomly generated dynamic-priority task sets under different values of the utilization factor and the maximum object usage ratio. In Figure 3, we first fixed the maxOU R to 0.3 and varied the utilization factor f between 0.1 to 1. The results shown that the energy consumption of all evaluated approaches grew with utilization factors. The performance ranking is MPS, IMS, BPS, and IASA (from the worst to the best). The MPS algorithm is the worst compared to others because it always executes tasks at the maximum processor speed s max . The BPS algorithm outperforms the MPS algorithm in most cases because it uses the base processor speed s b = min
Ci+ρ * Ti ≤ s j } for task executions, which is lower than s max when f is low. However, s b will be equal to s max when f is high enough.
As the result, in Figure 3, the energy consumption of the BPS algorithm is the same as that of the MPS when f ≥ 0.9.

Compared with the MPS and the BPS, the IASA consumes less energy in most cases. It is because the IASA use processor speeds lower than the base processor speed s b to execute tasks when there is no interference occurs. The IMS algorithm is designed for tasks with lock-based objects and it uses the SRP as its concurrency control protocol. The IMS uses a low speed s L for task executions and switches to a high speed s m whenever a task is blocked by τ m . Since s L ≤ s m ≤ s max , the IMS outperforms the MPS. However, it consumes more energy than that of the BPS and our proposed IASA algorithms. Note that the execution speeds of tasks scheduled by the IMS are highly related to the worst-case blocking time of tasks (as shown in Equation ( 6)), and the execution speeds of the BPS and the IASA are related to the worst-case execution time of a retry loop, i.e., ρ * = 4ms. Since the worst-case blocking time is relatively large than ρ * , tasks scheduled by the IMS algorithm might be executed at a higher execution speed compared to that of the BPS and the IASA.

V. CONCLUSION Energy-efficient DVS scheduling of real-time tasks has attracted widespread attention in the recent decade. In this paper, we explored the energy-efficient scheduling and synchronizing of tasks (modeled by the well-known Liu and Laylnad's periodic real-time task model) with lock-free objects on a non-ideal DVS processor. When tasks are scheduled by the EDF policy, an algorithm, called interference-aware speed assignment (IASA) algorithm, is proposed to assign execution speeds to tasks. Based on the schedulability analysis with the retry loops for the accesses of lock-free objects, the IASA algorithm calculates proper processor speeds for task execution so that the energy consumption can be reduced without violating tasks' timing constraints. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first result in real-time scheduling and synchronization of tasks with lock-free objects in a nonideal DVS processor. The capability of the IASA algorithm has been evaluated by a series of experiments, and from which we have some encouraging results.
